planting.note: Broadcast on a firm, well-prepared seedbed in early fall or early spring; Ladino clover establishes a persistent, spreading perennial stand and tolerates wetter soils than most clovers, making it a good choice for low, moist ground.

directions: Broadcast inoculated seed at 2–4 lb/acre on a firm, weed-free seedbed no more than 1/4 inch deep; Ladino clover is a giant-type selection of white clover (Trifolium repens), bred for substantially larger leaves, taller growth, and heavier biomass and forage yield than common white or Dutch white clover, while retaining the same low, spreading, stoloniferous habit and strong nitrogen-fixing ability. It tolerates wetter soils and heavier grazing or mowing pressure than many other clovers, and its persistent perennial nature means a single planting can provide years of nitrogen-fixing groundcover, pollinator forage, and high-quality grazing without replanting. Widely used in permanent pasture mixes and as a living mulch between rows of perennial crops, it also draws heavy honeybee traffic during its long bloom period. A productive, versatile perennial legume for pasture, orchard understory, or long-term soil building, zone 4–9.
sources: Midwest Cover Crops Council field guide
University of Georgia Extension — Clover Species for Forage and Cover

planting.note: Drill or broadcast after last frost once soil has warmed above 60°F, into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun; forage-type soybean varieties are bred for maximum leafy biomass and re-growth after grazing or mowing rather than for grain yield.

directions: Drill inoculated seed 1–1.5 inches deep into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun; forage soybean grows quickly into a dense, leafy, nitrogen-fixing summer cover, producing substantially more biomass and better regrowth after cutting or grazing than standard grain soybean varieties, which are bred to concentrate resources into seed rather than leaf and stem growth. It is widely used as a high-protein warm-season grazing and hay crop, as a deer and wildlife food-plot planting, and as a soil-building green manure that can be mowed and incorporated multiple times through the summer before a fall cover crop or cash crop follows. Its rapid growth and dense canopy also suppress weeds effectively during the hottest part of the growing season. A productive, multi-purpose warm-season legume for pasture, wildlife, or soil-building use, zone 4–10.
sources: Midwest Cover Crops Council field guide
Oklahoma State University Extension — Forage Soybean Production

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in early fall 6–8 weeks before the first hard frost, or in early spring, into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun to partial shade; orchardgrass tolerates more shade than most pasture grasses, giving it its name from traditional use in the dappled light of orchard alleys.

directions: Drill seed 1/4–1/2 inch deep into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun to partial shade; establishes quickly and tolerates more shade than nearly any other common pasture or cover crop grass, a trait reflected in its name from long use as groundcover beneath orchard trees. Orchardgrass is a deep-rooted, long-lived, cool-season bunchgrass widely used across temperate North America as a high-quality hay and pasture grass, valued for its rapid spring growth, good regrowth after cutting or grazing, and reasonable drought tolerance once its root system is established. As a cover crop, it forms a dense, persistent sod useful for erosion control on slopes and waterways, and its shade tolerance makes it one of the few grasses well suited to groundcover beneath widely spaced fruit or nut trees, where full-sun grasses like bermudagrass or bahiagrass struggle. A versatile, shade-tolerant perennial grass for pasture, hay, or orchard-floor groundcover, zone 3–8.
sources: University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension — Orchardgrass Management
USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet — Orchardgrass

planting.note: Broadcast or drill after all frost danger has passed into warm soil in full sun; bahiagrass germinates slowly and unevenly, and stands often take a full season to fully establish, but once rooted it forms a durable, low-maintenance, deep-rooted sod that persists for years.

directions: Broadcast seed at 15–20 lb/acre into warm, well-prepared soil in full sun; slow to establish but exceptionally drought-tolerant, low-input, and persistent once rooted, thanks to a deep, extensive root system. Bahiagrass is a warm-season perennial grass widely planted across the Gulf South and Southeast as a durable pasture, hay, and erosion-control grass, particularly valued on poor, sandy, or infertile soils where few other forage grasses perform reliably. Its deep, tough root system makes it one of the most drought-resistant pasture grasses available in the region, and its low fertility requirements and tolerance of close, continuous grazing have made it a standard choice for Gulf Coast livestock pasture for decades. The characteristic seed heads, forked into a distinctive V or Y shape, are a recognizable feature of bahiagrass pastures throughout summer and fall. A tough, low-maintenance, long-lived grass for Gulf South pasture, roadside, or erosion-control plantings, zone 7–10.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bahiagrass Production
USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet — Bahiagrass

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in early fall 6–8 weeks before the first hard frost, or in early spring, into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun to light shade; tall fescue establishes a dense, deep-rooted sod that persists for many years once mature.

directions: Drill seed 1/4–1/2 inch deep into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun to light shade; tolerates more shade than most pasture and cover crop grasses, making it useful under widely spaced orchard trees. Tall fescue is a deep-rooted, cool-season perennial grass widely used across the transition zone and upper South as a persistent pasture and hay grass, valued for its tolerance of heavy grazing, foot traffic, drought, and a wide range of soil conditions once established. As a cover crop, it forms a dense, long-lived sod that provides excellent erosion control on slopes, waterways, and orchard alleys, and its deep root system builds soil structure and organic matter over time. Older common tall fescue varieties carry a fungal endophyte that can cause toxicity issues in grazing livestock — endophyte-free or novel-endophyte cultivars are recommended where livestock grazing is intended. A tough, versatile, long-lived grass for permanent pasture, erosion control, or shaded orchard groundcover, zone 4–8.
sources: University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension — Tall Fescue Management
USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet — Tall Fescue
